name: Dust masks and other unrated masks
summary: Thin one-strap 'nuisance' dust masks, plus surgical and cloth masks. None shows a NIOSH approval number, so none is a respirator, and none is designed to seal to your face.
uses: Nuisance, non-toxic dust only, such as dust in pig or poultry barns; it is hard to fit and clogs as your breath dampens it
Surgical masks retain large droplets, but they are not designed to fit tightly and don't stop small airborne particles
Does nothing against gas, vapour, the gases in smoke or carbon monoxide, and nothing in oxygen-poor air
Not enough for lead, mould, fibreglass or smoke: use a NIOSH-approved N95 or better, and a P100 or FFP3 for lead
Asbestos: leave it alone. OSHA bans filtering masks for asbestos work and wants a half mask with HEPA filters or better
Doubling up dust masks doesn't make them protective
identify: A thin cup or flat pad with one elastic strap (sometimes two) and a metal nose strip, sold for sanding, sweeping and 'nuisance dust'. Judge it by the printing, not the shape. The line is plain: a respirator has been tested and approved and shows an approval number; a mask has not, and is not designed to seal to your face (NIOSH N95 check; CCOHS healthcare; NIOSH wildfire smoke). A real US respirator has the maker's name, NIOSH, an approval number TC-84A-xxxx, a class such as N95 and a part number printed on the mask; if any of these is missing it is not NIOSH-approved and can't be relied on (NIOSH N95 check). European ones show EN 149 and FFP1, FFP2 or FFP3 (Centexbel FFP); Canadian-certified ones may show CA-N95 (Health Canada CSA notice). No marks at all means an unrated mask. One strap, or loops round the ears, is another warning: the EPA says such masks aren't made to seal and won't protect your lungs (EPA smoke factsheet). Surgical or procedure masks (flat, pleated, ear loops) are not respirators: they stop large droplets but don't seal or filter the finest particles (CCOHS healthcare). Cloth masks, bandanas and tissues are in the same group (NIOSH wildfire smoke). Careful: OSHA's rule uses 'dust mask' as another name for a filtering facepiece respirator (OSHA 1910.134), so a box saying 'dust mask' might hold real N95s. Trust the NIOSH marks, not the word.
test: Nothing you can test will make one safe for fine dust: it was never rated. First look again for NIOSH, a TC-84A number and a class like N95 printed on the mask itself, because a box labelled 'dust mask' may hold real respirators (NIOSH N95 check). If it really is unrated and you use it for coarse dust anyway, check that the strap still stretches and grips, the nose strip and any foam are intact, and the pad isn't torn, wet, mouldy or caked. Press the nose strip to shape, cover the front with both hands and breathe in, then out: air you feel at the nose or edges is going round the filter, not through it (NIOSH donning guide; EPA smoke factsheet). With one strap and no seal you should expect leaks. Bin it when it is damaged, soiled, wet or harder to breathe through (NIOSH shelf life; EPA smoke factsheet).

decay.note: Estimate. It never protected much; the single elastic strap and foam nose pad perish first, and loose ones in sheds, cars and drawers get damp, dirty or mouldy.

improvise: Do the dust-control steps first, mask or not: HSE calls masks and respirators the last line of defence (HSE EM6). Leave suspect asbestos alone: HSE says only people who are trained and properly equipped should work on it (HSE EM6). Better than this mask: any NIOSH-approved N95 or better, an FFP2 or FFP3, or a half or full mask with particle filters. For mould, CDC asks for at least a NIOSH-approved N95 (CDC mold cleanup). Look in hospitals and clinics, in hardware stores and pharmacies, which the EPA notes sell respirators (EPA smoke factsheet), and in homes with leftover pandemic or wildfire stock. If an unrated mask is all you have, use it only for coarse dust. Snug, layered fine fabric is a little better than loose cloth (CDC mask types), but NIOSH says cloth and surgical masks, bandanas (wet or dry) and tissues give little or no protection from very small particles (NIOSH wildfire smoke). Doubling up dust masks is useless (HSE EM6). Useless against gas and vapour: OSHA says a respirator designed to filter dust will not protect against gases, vapours or very small solid particles of fumes or smoke (OSHA App D). No mask of any kind helps where oxygen is low, such as silos, manure pits and tanks: Alberta says atmosphere-supplying respirators must be used there, and HSE says respirators must not be used in oxygen-deficient air (Alberta producers; HSE HSG53). Fire smoke carries gases a dust mask cannot stop (NIOSH wildfire smoke). For smoke, EPA says staying indoors is the most effective step, and HEPA-filtered air cleaners indoors also help (EPA smoke factsheet).
